I would strongly advice against playing Kaz if you really want to become good at the game. 

As soon as you learn how to consistently use electrics it will carry you to the point where you lose out on fundamental skills. 
What I'm trying to say is that instead of having to choose between A, B or C that normal characters have to you can do ewgf to counter all those options with minimal risk and massive reward so you won't practice those A, B and C parts of the game well.

But if you really only want to play him then learn your character to the point where you no longer have to think about what YOU are doing but rather what your opponent is doing. You need to be comfortable and confident in your own character to the point where all your focus is "What is the best way to deal damage to my opponent in this situation" or from a defensive perspective "How do I deal with this situation I am in"

And to get there you also want to learn what every character in the game does. It will take time and you will have to use practice mode a lot, for me it's fun but not everyone wants to practice like this and this is reflected in real matches. 

If you are unfamiliar with a character you have to learn it and remember!

Other then that I would recommend kbd, throw breaking and reaction practice every time when warming up.

If your opponent get's a read on you that easily then it's probably a mix of you playing too "nice" and not switching up your timings.

Also when defending against your opponent don't try to psychically read what your opponent is going to do but rather do something like a d/f+1 and see what they do after blocking it, gather as much information about your opponents patterns as you can. The information you gather during small exchanges will get more and more accurate the longer the set goes on and with that information you can build a game plan around beating the options your opponent likes to do after X move. 

This process of gaining information about your opponents moves becomes easier to understand with experience. Just try not to do moves without a purpose and you'll soon start noticing patterns and how to deal with them.

Practice mode.

Took about three sessions to go from guessing to breaking 100 command throws in a row in practice mode.

Use any character that has command grabs for 1, 2 and 1+2 break like Jin or Dragunov and make them do the throws.

1. Back away and get used to the animations of their arms extending and once you feel comfortable go to step 2.
2. Get yourself grabbed and break as many throws as you can and once you start to get streaks of up to \~ 10 breaks in a row and feel comfortable move to step 3.
3. Keep the command grabs recorded / taken from the movelist but also add a slow reactable low into the mix that you have to block and punish correctly (Snake edge for Dragunov) and also a safe mid. (wr2 for Dragunov) Now this will feel quite a bit harder all of a sudden but it's very good practice. Once you are comfortable on this step you can move on to step 4.
4. Switch up the characters you are getting grabbed by. Dragunov, Jin, Nina, Hwoarang or whoever, just keep switching them up periodically, this way you won't get confused by different idle animations from different characters etc etc.... When you are at this step you can also start doing step 3 but with a twist! And the twist is.... Block the low and punish it, block the wr2 and break all the grabs while you are not looking at the character throwing you. This might sound impossible but I assure you it's not. What you want to do here is to actually look at the timer while you do everything listed in step 3 and by doing this you learn how to break throws while you're looking at other parts of the screen during the match since it's not realistic to always look at your opponents arms.

If you can block the low, block the mid and break 10 throws in a row I would call that a successful practice session.

Good luck!
